course.title: Carpentry and Furniture Making
course.tagline: Build tables, chairs and shelves with wood, tools and clean joints.

days.title: Wood, Tools and Safety
days.goal: Know the main wood types and the safety rules for every tool.

video.title: What Kind of Wood Should You Build With? | WOODWORKING BASICS

steps: Lay out a saw, hammer, tape measure, square, drill and sandpaper and name each one.
Feel pine, plywood and hardwood and note which is soft, light or heavy.
Put on safety glasses and learn the rule: never cut toward your body.
Sweep your work area and set up a steady bench or table.
days.task: Make a tool list with the job each tool does.
days.challenge: Name every tool on your bench without looking at the list.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you pick up a saw?
options: Cut as fast as you can
Check the area is clear, wear safety glasses and clamp the wood
quiz.explain: Safety comes first: glasses on, wood clamped, hands clear of the blade.

quiz.q: Which wood is soft and easy for a beginner to cut?
quiz.explain: Pine is soft, light and cheap, so it is the best wood to learn on.

quiz.q: What does the grain of wood mean?
options: The direction the wood fibres run
quiz.explain: Grain is the direction of the fibres; you cut and sand along it.

days.title: Measure and Mark Like a Pro
days.goal: Measure twice and mark wood so your cuts come out right.

video.title: What Kind of Wood Should You Build With? | WOODWORKING BASICS

steps: Measure a board three times and write the number down each time.
Mark a cut line with a pencil and a square so the line is straight.
Mark an X on the waste side so you cut on the right side of the line.
Measure a diagonal across a rectangle to check it is square.
days.task: Mark and cut a board to exactly 30cm long.
days.challenge: Cut three boards to the same length with no gaps between them.

days.title: Sawing Straight by Hand
days.goal: Cut wood straight with a hand saw.

video.title: What Kind of Wood Should You Build With? | WOODWORKING BASICS

steps: Clamp the board firmly so it cannot move.
Start the cut with short gentle pulls, then use long smooth strokes.
Watch the line, not the blade, and keep the saw straight.
Sand the cut edge smooth with sandpaper.
days.task: Cut a board straight along a marked line with no wobble.
days.challenge: Cut a board so straight it needs no sanding.

days.title: Pocket-Hole Joints Made Easy
days.goal: Join two boards with a pocket hole, a strong hidden screw joint.

video.title: Beginner's Guide to Pocket Hole Joinery

steps: A pocket hole is a hole drilled at an angle so a screw can join two boards.
Clamp the pocket-hole jig (a guide that holds the drill at the right angle) to the board.
Drill the pocket holes, then drive screws through them into the second board.
Check the joint is tight and the screw heads sit hidden inside the holes.
days.task: Join two boards at a right angle with pocket holes.
days.challenge: Join two boards so the joint holds when you lift it by one end.

quiz.q: What is a pocket hole?
options: A hole drilled at an angle so a screw can join two boards
quiz.explain: A pocket hole lets a screw pull two boards together from a hidden angle.

quiz.q: Why use pocket holes?
options: They hide the screws and make a strong joint
quiz.explain: Pocket-hole screws sit inside the hole, so the joint is strong and the screws stay hidden.

quiz.q: What does the pocket-hole jig do?
options: It holds the drill at the right angle
quiz.explain: The jig is a guide that keeps the drill bit at the correct angle for the pocket hole.

days.title: Drilling Clean Holes
days.goal: Drill straight, clean holes without splitting the wood.

video.title: Beginner's Guide to Pocket Hole Joinery

steps: Mark the hole spot with a pencil cross.
Start the drill slowly so the bit does not wander.
Drill straight down and pull the bit out often to clear the dust.
Put a scrap board underneath so the back does not split.
days.task: Drill six clean holes in a row with no splitting.
days.challenge: Drill a hole exactly where you marked it, first try.

days.title: Screws, Glue and Clamps
days.goal: Hold wood together with screws, glue and clamps the right way.

video.title: Beginner's Guide to Pocket Hole Joinery

steps: Spread a thin even layer of wood glue on one joining face.
Press the boards together and wipe off glue that squeezes out.
Add screws while the glue is wet, then clamp the joint tight.
Leave the clamp on until the glue dries fully.
days.task: Glue and screw two boards together and test the joint the next day.
days.challenge: Glue a joint with no glue mess on the outside.

days.title: Project: Build a Small Wooden Box
days.goal: Build a small open wooden box with glued and screwed joints.

video.title: Wood Joinery Basics

steps: Cut four sides and a bottom from one board.
Glue and screw the sides into a rectangle, checking the corners are square.
Fix the bottom on with screws from underneath.
Sand every edge smooth and check the box sits flat.
days.task: Finish a small wooden box that sits flat and holds its shape.
days.challenge: Build the box with all four corners perfectly square.

quiz.q: What is a butt joint?
options: Two boards pushed end to face and fixed
Two boards glued edge to edge
quiz.explain: A butt joint is the simplest joint: the end of one board meets the face of another.

quiz.q: What is a mitre joint?
options: Two boards cut at 45 degrees and joined at a corner
quiz.explain: Mitre joints meet at 45 degrees, like the corners of a picture frame.

quiz.q: Why use wood glue as well as screws?
options: Glue spreads the load and makes the joint much stronger
quiz.explain: Glue bonds the whole joining face, so the joint is stronger than screws alone.

days.title: Sanding Smooth
days.goal: Sand wood through the grits until it feels smooth.

video.title: Wood Joinery Basics

steps: Sandpaper grit is the roughness number: low numbers are rough, high numbers are fine.
Start with rough 80-grit paper, then 120, then 220.
Sand with the grain (the direction the wood lines run), never across it.
Wipe the dust off with a cloth and feel the surface with your hand.
days.task: Sand one board smooth enough to run your hand over with no roughness.
days.challenge: Sand a box inside and out with no rough spots left.

days.title: Joints: Butt, Lap and Mitre
days.goal: Make three basic joints and know when to use each one.

video.title: Wood Joinery Basics

steps: A butt joint is two boards pushed end to face; glue and screw it.
A lap joint overlaps two boards halfway; cut a notch in each one.
A mitre joint joins two boards cut at 45 degrees, like a picture frame.
Glue all three joints and test which one is strongest.
days.task: Make one of each joint and label them.
days.challenge: Make a mitre joint with no gap at the corner.

days.title: Plan an End Table

video.title: How to Build an Easy End Table

steps: Sketch the table from the front and the side.
Write the length, width and height of every part.
List the boards you need and how many of each.
Check the height works next to a real chair or sofa.
days.task: Draw a measured plan for an end table.
days.challenge: Plan a table using only boards you already have.

quiz.q: What is the apron of a table?
options: The frame under the tabletop that joins the legs
quiz.explain: The apron is the frame below the top; it holds the legs together and stops wobble.

quiz.q: Why check the diagonals of a frame?
options: To check the frame is square
quiz.explain: If both diagonals are equal, the frame is square; if not, it is leaning.

quiz.q: How do you stop a table wobbling?
options: Check it is square and trim the long leg
quiz.explain: A wobble usually means one leg is longer; trimming it levels the table.

quiz.q: Why sand between coats of finish?

quiz.q: What does 2x4 mean?
options: A board about 2 inches by 4 inches
quiz.explain: 2x4 is the size name for a common thick board, about 2 by 4 inches.

quiz.q: Why are 2x4 projects good for beginners?
options: The wood is cheap, strong and easy to cut and join
quiz.explain: 2x4 timber is cheap and forgiving, so beginners can build real furniture with it.

quiz.q: What should you check before buying 2x4 boards?
options: That the boards are straight with no big bends
quiz.explain: Bent or twisted boards make wobbly furniture, so pick straight ones.

days.title: Stools: Legs and Angles

video.title: I Built a Wooden Stool — Easy DIY Anyone Can Make

quiz.q: What are splayed legs?
options: Legs that angle outward from the top
quiz.explain: Splayed legs angle outward, which makes a stool much harder to tip over.

quiz.q: What do stretchers do on a stool?
options: Bars between the legs that stop wobble and add strength
quiz.explain: Stretchers tie the legs together so the stool stays stiff and steady.

quiz.q: How do you test a stool you just built?
options: Sit on it and rock it gently to check it is strong and steady
quiz.explain: Sitting and rocking tests the joints under real weight before anyone else uses it.

days.title: Finish a Tabletop
days.goal: Stain and seal a tabletop so it looks good and resists spills.

video.title: How to Build a DIY Dining Table

steps: Sand the top smooth up to 220-grit paper.
Wipe on stain evenly and let it dry.
Brush or wipe on a clear sealer in thin coats.
Sand lightly between coats and add a second coat.
days.task: Finish a tabletop with an even stain and smooth sealer.
days.challenge: Fix a patchy stain by sanding back and starting again.

quiz.q: How do you join boards into a wide tabletop?
options: Nail them on top of each other
Glue them edge to edge and clamp them flat
Screw them to the legs only
quiz.explain: Edge-gluing boards side by side makes one wide flat top.

quiz.q: Why clamp a tabletop while the glue dries?
options: To hold the boards flat and tight so the top has no gaps
quiz.explain: Clamps press the boards together and keep them flat while the glue sets.

quiz.q: Why screw the top on from underneath?
options: So no screw heads show on the top surface
quiz.explain: Screws from below keep the tabletop smooth and clean on top.

video.title: How to Build a Farmhouse Kitchen Table

steps: Look at farmhouse tables and note the thick legs and wide top.
Choose a warm stain colour that suits the style.
Learn how an apron under the top adds strength and looks.
Sketch your own farmhouse table.
days.task: Sketch a farmhouse table with labels for each part.
days.challenge: Name three things that make a table look farmhouse style.

capstone.title: Build a Small Table or Shelf for a Real Home
capstone.brief: Design and build a small table or shelf for a real room in a home, finished, level and strong, and present it with a costing sheet.
checks: Piece designed from real measurements of the room
Piece stands level with no wobble
Sanded smooth with no splinters or rough spots
Finish even: stain or sealer applied neatly
Costing sheet shows wood, screws, glue, time and selling price
deliverables: Finished table or shelf, level and strong
Four photos: front, side, back and top
